terms.definition: A Linux configuration file that lists scheduled commands (cron jobs) for the cron daemon to execute automatically at specified times.
terms.example: A crontab entry '0 2 * * *' means run a backup script every day at 2:00 AM.

terms.definition: A background process in Linux that wakes up every minute, reads the crontab file, and executes any jobs whose scheduled time matches the current time.
terms.example: The cron daemon automatically runs your backup.sh script at 2 AM without any human interaction.

terms.definition: A 5-field time pattern used in crontab to specify when a job should run: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, and day-of-week.
terms.example: '*/5 * * * *' runs a job every 5 minutes. '0 9 * * 1-5' runs at 9 AM every weekday.

terms.definition: A data structure in the Linux file system that stores metadata about a file (size, permissions, owner, disk location) but NOT the file name itself.
terms.example: When you run ls -li, the first number shown is the inode number. Two files with the same inode share the same data.

terms.definition: An additional directory entry pointing to the same inode as an existing file. Both names reference the exact same data on disk, and the data persists as long as any hard link exists.
terms.example: ln original.txt backup.txt creates a hard link. Even if original.txt is deleted, backup.txt still works.

terms.definition: A symbolic link — a special file that stores only the path to another file, acting like a shortcut. If the target file is moved or deleted, the soft link breaks.
terms.example: ln -s /home/user/config.txt /root/config is a soft link. ls -l shows it starting with 'l' and pointing to the target.

terms.definition: Another name for a soft link — a file containing only a path reference to another file or directory. Identified by 'l' at the start of ls -l output.
terms.example: Linux config files often use symlinks: /etc/alternatives/java -> /usr/lib/jvm/java-11/bin/java

terms.definition: The Linux command for creating links. Without flags it creates a hard link; with -s flag it creates a soft (symbolic) link.
terms.example: ln file.txt hardlink.txt (hard link) | ln -s /path/file.txt /root/shortcut.txt (soft link)

terms.definition: A Linux command that lists files with their inode numbers and detailed metadata. Used to verify whether two files share the same inode (hard links).
terms.example: If original.txt and backup.txt both show inode 1234567, they are hard links pointing to the same data.

terms.definition: Web GET — a non-interactive Linux command-line tool for downloading files from the internet. Supports HTTP, HTTPS, and FTP. Ideal for scripts and automated downloads.
terms.example: wget https://example.com/setup.tar.gz downloads the file to the current directory.

terms.definition: Client URL — a versatile command-line data transfer tool supporting HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SFTP, and more. Can send any HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) with custom headers and request bodies.
terms.example: curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"key":"value"}' https://api.example.com

terms.definition: A special HTTP endpoint at 169.254.169.254 accessible only from inside an EC2 instance that provides instance information like instance ID, AMI ID, region, and IAM role credentials.
terms.example: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id returns the current EC2 instance's ID.

terms.definition: An AWS serverless event bus service that uses cron expressions (and rate expressions) to schedule automated AWS actions like triggering Lambda functions or stopping EC2 instances.
terms.example: A cron expression 'cron(0 2 * * ? *)' in EventBridge runs a Lambda function every day at 2 AM UTC.

terms.definition: A Linux shell command that creates an environment variable and makes it available to all child processes launched from the current terminal session.
terms.example: export EDITOR=nano makes all programs in this terminal (including crontab -e) use nano as the default editor.

terms.definition: A named value stored in the shell's environment that processes can read. Used to configure program behavior without changing code.
terms.example: EDITOR=nano, PATH=/usr/bin:/bin, HOME=/home/ec2-user are all environment variables.

terms.definition: A soft link that points to a file or path that no longer exists. Also called a broken link. Attempting to access it returns 'No such file or directory'.
terms.example: If you create a soft link to config.txt and then delete config.txt, the soft link becomes dangling (broken) and turns red in ls -l output.

terms.definition: The >> operator in Linux that redirects command output to the END of a file, preserving existing content. Contrast with > (overwrite) which replaces the file contents.
terms.example: echo "Job ran" >> cron.log appends each message. Using > instead would delete previous entries each time.

terms.definition: A Linux command that adds execute (x) permission to a file, making it runnable as a script or program.
terms.example: chmod +x script.sh makes script.sh executable so crontab can run it with the command /home/ec2-user/script.sh.

terms.definition: The number of hard links pointing to an inode, shown in ls -l output as the second column. When this count reaches zero, the inode and data are freed from disk.
terms.example: A file with link count 2 has two hard links. Deleting one reduces count to 1; the data remains. Deleting both frees the disk space.

terms.definition: A crontab notation using */ followed by a number to mean 'every N units'. Used to create regular interval schedules.
terms.example: */5 in the minutes field = every 5 minutes. */6 in the hours field = every 6 hours (at 0, 6, 12, 18).

terms.definition: A log file used to capture output from cron jobs, typically created using the append operator >> in the shell script being scheduled.
terms.example: echo "$(date): Job ran" >> /home/ec2-user/cron.log creates a timestamped log entry each time the cron job executes.
